name: Erik Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the supermarket in the town where I grew up, the one by the old railway bridge. I'm on the tills most of the day, and in the afternoons I do the beer and wine aisle and bring the trolleys in from the car park. I've been there just under a year, after a few years doing odd jobs, so I'm still learning the codes and the age checks. Half the customers knew my dad, so I can't have a bad day without someone mentioning it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work and people say thank you. What wears me out is the car park in the rain, and the self-checkouts calling me over every five minutes because someone's put a bag of carrots in the wrong place. I'm engaged to Sara, who's a hairdresser, and we're getting married next September, so every penny is going into the wedding pot. Sundays are church, then dinner at my mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. At work I'd tell the lads the computers were never going to do an honest day's work. I don't post online, so it'd be at the pub, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my worries don't go anywhere. The wedding's costing about nine thousand, and we've got three months of savings plus the wedding pot. The shop keeps adding self-checkouts whether AI is hype or not, and every new one means one less shift for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, work hard and try to get on the beer and wine supervisor rota, because that's a small step up. I'd keep the wedding savings going, about two hundred a month between us. I wouldn't change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not about the robots, about money. Weddings and rent don't care about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the extra shifts dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the honeymoon. We were thinking of a week by the sea, but a few nights at Sara's aunt's place would do. The wedding itself we won't cut, because both families have been waiting for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good worker look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard work, mostly, and doing what your manager tells you even when you don't like it. My dad worked at the brewery for thirty years and never missed a shift. That's what I'd want people to say about me.

say: I'd tell the lads the computers were never going to do **an honest day's work**.
I'd say it **at the pub**, since I don't post online.
think: My worries are **money**, with a wedding costing about **nine thousand**.
New **self-checkouts** keep cutting shifts whether AI is hype or not.
do: Get onto the **beer and wine supervisor** rota.
Keep saving about **£200 a month** with Sara for the wedding.
S0.quote: Weddings and rent don't care about AI.
fieldNote: Erik's real pressure is a **£9,000 wedding** and shifts lost to self-checkouts.
He defines himself by **hard work**, modelled on his father's brewery job.
He would cut the **honeymoon** before the wedding itself, to honour both families.

steps.text: Ask to join the beer and wine supervisor rota
Keep putting two hundred a month into the wedding pot
Swap the seaside honeymoon for nights at Sara's aunt's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people running these big chains have never stood behind a till. At work I'd say keep your head down and be the best at what you do. I wouldn't be signing petitions or anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking work going to computers doesn't touch me much at first, it's the office lot at head office. But the shop would get told to do more with fewer staff, and the rota computer would decide who gets the shifts. I'm new and I'm slow on the codes, so I'm not top of anyone's list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder and ask for every extra shift going. I'd talk to my uncle Tarek about whether there's room on his roofing crew, just as a backup. And Sara and I would probably cut the wedding guest list to keep the cost down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, if I'm honest. Like when the boss calls you into the office and you don't know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't see the point. My phone does what I need, calls and football scores. If the shop makes me learn something, I'll learn it, but I'm not going home to play with chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Roofing is a big switch. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, roofing is proper work. My uncle Tarek has been on roofs for twenty-five years and he's never short of jobs. It's hard on your knees, but nobody's putting a robot on a slate roof in the rain anytime soon.

say: I'd say the people running **big chains** have never stood behind a till.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep your head down** and be the best.
think: Thinking AI hits **head office** first, then shops do more with fewer staff.
The **rota computer** decides shifts, and I'm new and slow on codes.
do: Ask my uncle about a place on his **roofing crew**.
Cut the **wedding guest list** to save money.
feel: **Worried**, like being called into **the boss's office**.
S1.quote: Nobody's putting a robot on a slate roof in the rain anytime soon.
fieldNote: Erik **refuses AI tools** outright but would learn if the shop required it.
His fallback is **family**: his uncle's roofing crew, not a course.
He blames **chain bosses** who never worked a till, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Ask the manager for every spare till shift
Ask Uncle Tarek about joining his roofing crew
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred twenty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and someone in charge should have stopped it. But I wouldn't want handouts, I'd want proper work and apprenticeships. I'd say that at church and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's frightening. The computers take the office jobs in 2028, and then everybody comes looking for work like mine. Around 2031 the robots come for the tills, the shelves and the trolleys, and I'd be thirty with nothing but shop work and a wedding ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with my uncle Tarek's roofing crew straight away, even on apprentice pay, and keep the shop job weekends. I'd ask Sara if we can do a smaller wedding, maybe just the church and a hall. We'd save everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared. I've never been one to panic, but this one keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your fiancée Sara say to each other that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara would say the wedding goes ahead no matter what, and she's right. We'd just make it smaller. My mum would offer to help with the food, and Sara's family would chip in. That's what families do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why roofing, if robots come for hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roofs are harder for a robot than tills. If the robots can do hands-on work by 2031, maybe roofs take a bit longer, I don't know. I'd rather be on a roof than waiting at a supermarket till for a letter.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and someone in charge should have stopped it.
I'd want **apprenticeships**, not handouts, and say so at church.
think: After **2028**, office workers chase jobs like mine.
Around **2031**, robots take tills, shelves and trolleys when I'm thirty.
do: Join the **roofing crew** on apprentice pay and keep weekend shop shifts.
Shrink the **wedding** to the church and a hall.
S2.quote: I'd rather be on a roof than waiting at a supermarket till for a letter.
fieldNote: Erik's traditional values show: **family help**, not government help.
He bets on roofing lasting **a little longer** than shop work, but admits uncertainty.
The **wedding** goes ahead, just smaller, which matters deeply to him.

steps.text: Start on Uncle Tarek's roofing crew at apprentice pay
Hold a small church wedding with a hall
Save every spare pound after the wedding
Accept mum's help cooking for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so learn a trade and don't wait for the government. At church I'd say look after each other. That's the right way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably wait a year or two, see if it's real. Robots in the shop around 2034 means I'd be thirty-four, and that's a long time to be on a roof if I don't have to be. But I know waiting is a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shop job and get married next September as planned. Then maybe in 2028 I'd start on my uncle's roofing crew part-time. I'd keep saving about a hundred a month after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like knowing the car needs fixing and putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep the wedding as planned in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd keep it, because the families have been waiting. In the fast picture I'd make it smaller. In this one we'd keep it as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the news, that's for sure. When I see robots actually doing a supermarket shift in a real shop near us, I'd go to my uncle the next week.

say: I'd say **learn a trade** and don't wait for the government.
I'd tell people at church to **look after each other**.
think: I'd probably **wait** a year or two to see if it's real.
Robots around **2034** gives time, but I know waiting is a **gamble**.
do: Keep the **shop job** and marry next September as planned.
Start **roofing part-time** with my uncle around 2028.
Save about **£100 a month** after the wedding.
S3.quote: When I see robots actually doing a supermarket shift in a real shop near us, I'd go to my uncle the next week.
fieldNote: Erik's **resistance** shows as waiting for proof he can see himself.
The **wedding** stays as planned with five years' warning.
He still expects to **lose the shop job**, so he remains anxious.

steps.text: Stay at the supermarket and marry next September
Start part-time on the roofing crew around 2028
Save a hundred a month after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough for anyone to sort themselves out. At work I'd say there's no need to panic. I'd say the same at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine for a long while. Robots on the shop floor around 2039, I'd be forty, and maybe a supervisor by then, or on the roofs with my uncle. I'd still rather it didn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shop job and work toward supervisor. We'd get married next year and maybe think about a baby in a couple of years. Later on, maybe around 2033, I'd look at roofing seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not much. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really plan a family with this coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If we wait for the world to be safe, we'd never have kids. My parents had me when things were hard too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to look after in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum and dad, mostly. They'd be in their seventies by then, and I'd want to be able to look after them. That's my job as their son.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for anyone to sort themselves out.
I'd tell colleagues and church there's **no need to panic**.
think: Robots around **2039** means I'd be forty, maybe a **supervisor** by then.
I'd still rather it **didn't happen** at all.
do: Marry next year and think about **a baby** in a couple of years.
feel: **Uneasy**, but only a little, since it's a **long way** off.
S4.quote: If we wait for the world to be safe, we'd never have kids.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Erik keep **family plans** firmly on track.
His sense of duty extends to **ageing parents**.
He'd only consider **roofing** later, staying loyal to the shop.

steps.text: Work toward the supervisor role at the supermarket
Marry Sara next year and plan a baby
Look at joining the roofing crew around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time, a wedding to pay for and no trade. What would help is proper apprenticeships for people my age, paid enough to live on, not benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. That's where people would turn first if this happened, not the government. Our church already runs a food bank, and the food bank would get a lot busier.

headlineQuote: Our church already runs a food bank, and the food bank would get a lot busier.
portrait: Erik is **27**, a junior cashier and trolley collector at the supermarket in his **home town**.
He's engaged to Sara, a hairdresser, and saving for a **£9,000 wedding**.
He never uses AI and **waits for proof** before acting.
His fallback is his uncle's **roofing crew**, and he wants apprenticeships, not handouts.
His mood swings from **alarmed** at 2028 to only mildly uneasy at 2036.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with a wedding to pay for and no trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people his age, not benefits.
